claim: More than 430 million people worldwide, approximately 5% of the world's population, live with disabling hearing loss.
source: More than 430 million people worldwide, ~5% of the world's population, live with disabling hearing loss, making it the most common sensory deficit (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: Disabling hearing loss is the most common sensory deficit.
source: More than 430 million people worldwide, ~5% of the world's population, live with disabling hearing loss, making it the most common sensory deficit (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: The WHO estimates that the number of people with disabling hearing loss will grow to 700 million by 2050.
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that this number will grow to 700 million by 2050 (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: There are significant associations between hearing impairment and reduced quality of life.
source: There are significant associations between hearing impairment and reduced quality of life, increased risk for dementia, and/or an inability to function independently (Gurgel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gurgel et al., 2014

claim: There are significant associations between hearing impairment and increased risk for dementia.
source: There are significant associations between hearing impairment and reduced quality of life, increased risk for dementia, and/or an inability to function independently (Gurgel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gurgel et al., 2014

claim: There are significant associations between hearing impairment and an inability to function independently.
source: There are significant associations between hearing impairment and reduced quality of life, increased risk for dementia, and/or an inability to function independently (Gurgel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gurgel et al., 2014

claim: In sensorineural hearing loss, there is often a loss of sensory hair cells that transduce sound-induced vibrations within the cochlea into neural activity.
source: In the most common type of hearing loss, called sensorineural hearing loss, there is often a loss of the sensory hair cells that transduce sound-induced vibrations within the cochlea into neural activity; this loss precludes the use of sound-amplifying hearing aids as a potential treatment.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about sensorineural hearing loss

claim: Loss of hair cells precludes the use of sound-amplifying hearing aids as a potential treatment.
source: In the most common type of hearing loss, called sensorineural hearing loss, there is often a loss of the sensory hair cells that transduce sound-induced vibrations within the cochlea into neural activity; this loss precludes the use of sound-amplifying hearing aids as a potential treatment.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hearing aid limitations

claim: A cochlear implant can be implanted to electrically stimulate spiral ganglion neurons.
source: Instead, a cochlear implant (CI) can be implanted to electrically stimulate spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the neurons downstream from hair cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cochlear implants

claim: Spiral ganglion neurons are the neurons downstream from hair cells.
source: Instead, a cochlear implant (CI) can be implanted to electrically stimulate spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the neurons downstream from hair cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about auditory anatomy

claim: CIs are generally effective for enabling speech comprehension, with mean single syllable open set word recognition scores of 65% in quiet.
source: CIs are generally effective for enabling speech comprehension, with mean single syllable open set word recognition scores of 65% in quiet (Firszt et al., 2004; Holden et al., 2013; Moberly et al., 2016a, Moberly et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: There is a significant reduction in CI performance when background noise levels are high.
source: However, there is a significant reduction in CI performance when background noise levels are high and most CI users also cannot appreciate music (Friesen et al., 2001; Jiam et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friesen et al., 2001 and Jiam et al., 2017

claim: Most CI users cannot appreciate music.
source: However, there is a significant reduction in CI performance when background noise levels are high and most CI users also cannot appreciate music (Friesen et al., 2001; Jiam et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friesen et al., 2001 and Jiam et al., 2017

claim: The limitations in CI performance are thought to arise largely from the small number of independent spectral channels created by CIs.
source: The limitations in performance are thought to arise largely from the small number of independent spectral channels created by CIs.
evidence: Based on inference from the scientific literature and context

claim: The intact human cochlea has approximately 30,000 spiral ganglion neurons.
source: In contrast to the large number of independent channels arising from the ~30,000 SGNs in the intact human cochlea, CIs produce as few as 8–10 independent spectral channels (Friesen et al., 2001; Fishman et al., 1997; Fu and Nogaki, 2005; Carlyon et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about human cochlear anatomy

claim: CIs produce as few as 8-10 independent spectral channels.
source: In contrast to the large number of independent channels arising from the ~30,000 SGNs in the intact human cochlea, CIs produce as few as 8–10 independent spectral channels (Friesen et al., 2001; Fishman et al., 1997; Fu and Nogaki, 2005; Carlyon et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The number of independent spectral channels from CIs is smaller than the number of stimulating electrodes in most existing devices.
source: This is smaller than the number of stimulating electrodes in most existing devices (Fishman et al., 1997; Friesen et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fishman et al., 1997 and Friesen et al., 2001

claim: The high conductivity of the perilymph within the scala tympani leads to an expansive spread of current in the longitudinal direction.
source: For example, the high conductivity of the perilymph within the scala tympani leads to an expansive spread of current in the longitudinal direction (along the tonotopic axis; Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on established biophysical principles and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: The high electrical resistance of the bony wall separating the scala tympani from targeted SGNs within the organ of Corti necessitates an increase in the amplitude of stimulation.
source: In addition, the high electrical resistance of the bony wall separating the scala tympani from targeted SGNs within the organ of Corti necessitates an increase in the amplitude of stimulation that results in an even wider spread of activation.
evidence: Based on established biophysical principles

claim: Increased stimulation amplitude results in an even wider spread of activation.
source: In addition, the high electrical resistance of the bony wall separating the scala tympani from targeted SGNs within the organ of Corti necessitates an increase in the amplitude of stimulation that results in an even wider spread of activation.
evidence: Based on logical inference from biophysical principles

claim: Excessive spread from individual electrodes can result in overlap of fields from neighboring electrodes, thereby reducing spectral specificity.
source: Excessive spread from individual electrodes can result in overlap of fields from neighboring electrodes, thereby reducing spectral specificity.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the described physical phenomena

claim: Genetic insertion of light-sensitive ion channels into SGNs allows their activation to be controlled by light, resulting in narrower channels.
source: For example, the genetic insertion of light-sensitive ion channels into SGNs allows their activation to be controlled by light instead of electric fields, resulting in narrower channels (Hernandez et al., 2014 ; Dieter et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hernandez et al., 2014 and Dieter et al., 2019

claim: Electrode arrays that penetrate directly into the auditory nerve enable better control of activation of the central axons of SGNs.
source: Another approach uses electrode arrays that penetrate directly into the auditory nerve (Middlebrooks and Snyder, 2007; Middlebrooks and Snyder, 2008; Middlebrooks and Snyder, 2010); the reduced separation between electrodes and targeted neurons, along with the elimination of the high-resistance barrier, enables better control of activation of the central axons of SGNs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Middlebrooks and Snyder studies and logical inference

claim: Magnetic stimulation from small, implantable coils (micro-coils) can effectively drive neurons of the central nervous system while confining activation to a narrow region around each coil.
source: Recent studies have shown that magnetic stimulation from small, implantable coils, referred to as micro-coils, can effectively drive neurons of the central nervous system (CNS) while confining activation to a narrow region around each coil (Lee et al., 2016; Lee and Fried, 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Ryu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Magnetic fields are highly permeable to most biological materials.
source: A coil-based approach is potentially attractive for CIs because magnetic fields are highly permeable to most biological materials, for example, the bony walls of the scala tympani, and thus activation of SGN processes would not require the same increase in stimulation amplitude required for electric stimulation.
evidence: Based on established physical principles of magnetic fields

claim: The spread of magnetic fields in the scala tympani is less sensitive to the high conductivity of perilymph.
source: Further, the spread of magnetic fields in the scala tympani is less sensitive to the high conductivity of perilymph, further helping to confine activation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on physical principles and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Computational studies suggest that the spatial gradient of the fields induced by micro-coils is suprathreshold.
source: While the strength of the fields induced by micro-coils is small, computational studies suggest that the spatial gradient of the resulting fields is suprathreshold (Lee et al., 2016; Lee and Fried, 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Osanai et al., 2018; Minusa et al., 2018; Ryu et al., 2020), and simulations specific to the cochlea suggest a multiturn spiral coil should produce fields strong enough to activate SGNs (Mukesh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple computational studies

claim: Simulations specific to the cochlea suggest a multiturn spiral coil should produce fields strong enough to activate SGNs.
source: While the strength of the fields induced by micro-coils is small, computational studies suggest that the spatial gradient of the resulting fields is suprathreshold (Lee et al., 2016; Lee and Fried, 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Osanai et al., 2018; Minusa et al., 2018; Ryu et al., 2020), and simulations specific to the cochlea suggest a multiturn spiral coil should produce fields strong enough to activate SGNs (Mukesh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukesh et al., 2017

claim: Simple bends in microwires have been shown to be effective for the activation of CNS neurons.
source: Instead, simple bends in microwires, recently shown to be effective for the activation of CNS neurons (Lee et al., 2016; Lee and Fried, 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Ryu et al., 2020), may offer an attractive alternative to multiturn spiral coil designs because they allow coil sizes to be minimized, and thus the flexibility and overall structure of coil-based CIs can be made to match existing implants, thereby reducing a barrier to implementation.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Bent-wire micro-coils can drive the auditory pathways.
source: Here, we investigate the ability of magnetic stimulation from bent-wire micro-coils to drive the auditory pathways.
evidence: This is the primary research question being investigated in the study

claim: Bent-wire micro-coils can drive auditory circuits effectively.
source: We show that bent-wire micro-coils can indeed drive auditory circuits effectively and further, that the resulting activation from single micro-coils is significantly narrower than that from traditional electrodes, that is, approaching the relatively narrow spread produced by acoustic stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The resulting activation from single micro-coils is significantly narrower than that from traditional electrodes.
source: We show that bent-wire micro-coils can indeed drive auditory circuits effectively and further, that the resulting activation from single micro-coils is significantly narrower than that from traditional electrodes, that is, approaching the relatively narrow spread produced by acoustic stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The activation from single micro-coils approaches the relatively narrow spread produced by acoustic stimuli.
source: We show that bent-wire micro-coils can indeed drive auditory circuits effectively and further, that the resulting activation from single micro-coils is significantly narrower than that from traditional electrodes, that is, approaching the relatively narrow spread produced by acoustic stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Control experiments verified that responses from coils were indeed magnetic in origin.
source: Control experiments verified that responses from coils were indeed magnetic in origin and that they did not arise from activation of hair cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from control experiments

claim: Responses from coils did not arise from activation of hair cells.
source: Control experiments verified that responses from coils were indeed magnetic in origin and that they did not arise from activation of hair cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from control experiments

claim: Coil-based stimulation may produce a larger number of independent spectral channels than electrode-based CIs.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that further investigation of coil-based CIs is warranted as they may produce a larger number of independent spectral channels than electrode-based CIs and thus could lead to improved clinical outcomes.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data presented

claim: Coil-based CIs could lead to improved clinical outcomes.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that further investigation of coil-based CIs is warranted as they may produce a larger number of independent spectral channels than electrode-based CIs and thus could lead to improved clinical outcomes.
evidence: Based on speculation from the experimental data

claim: Acoustic stimuli consisted of single frequencies ranging from 8 to 48 kHz.
source: Acoustic stimuli consisted of a series of single frequencies ranging from 8 to 48 kHz, chosen to cover much of the tonotopic range represented in the central division of the mouse IC (Stiebler and Ehret, 1985).
evidence: Describes the experimental methods used in the study

claim: The frequency range 8 to 48 kHz covers much of the tonotopic range represented in the central division of the mouse IC.
source: Acoustic stimuli consisted of a series of single frequencies ranging from 8 to 48 kHz, chosen to cover much of the tonotopic range represented in the central division of the mouse IC (Stiebler and Ehret, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stiebler and Ehret, 1985

claim: MUAs typically have 'V'-shaped tuning curves.
source: The MUAs, which are combined responses from single-unit activities with various tuning curves, typically have 'V'-shaped tuning curves (Snyder et al., 2008) and MUA-based STCs for acoustic stimulation also have narrow 'V'-shaped curves; examples for 8, 16, and 32 kHz are shown in Figure 2A–C, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Snyder et al., 2008 and illustrated in Figure 2A-C

claim: Only 5 out of 11 animals had best sites at 8 kHz.
source: Only 5 out of 11 animals had best sites at 8 kHz (Figure 2D) and thus the sampling of the lowest frequency region of the IC may have been incomplete.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The sampling of the lowest frequency region of the IC may have been incomplete.
source: Only 5 out of 11 animals had best sites at 8 kHz (Figure 2D) and thus the sampling of the lowest frequency region of the IC may have been incomplete.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data

claim: Increases in suprathreshold sound pressure levels typically led to increases in the magnitude of the IC response before saturating at higher intensity levels.
source: Consistent with previous studies, increases in suprathreshold sound pressure levels (SPLs) typically led to increases in the magnitude of the IC response before saturating at higher intensity levels (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and consistent with previous studies

claim: The dynamic range for acoustic stimulation averaged 25.96 ± 9.17 dB.
source: The dynamic range (DR), defined as the range of stimulus amplitudes for which response strength was between 10% and 90% of the maximum response at BS, averaged 25.96 ± 9.17 dB (Figure 6D), consistent with previous reports in mice (Köppl and Yates, 1999; Nizami, 2002; Shivdasani et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The dynamic range for acoustic stimulation is consistent with previous reports in mice.
source: The dynamic range (DR), defined as the range of stimulus amplitudes for which response strength was between 10% and 90% of the maximum response at BS, averaged 25.96 ± 9.17 dB (Figure 6D), consistent with previous reports in mice (Köppl and Yates, 1999; Nizami, 2002; Shivdasani et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in mice

claim: Distilled water was injected through the round window membrane to induce an osmotic shock to the hair cells.
source: For lesioning, distilled water was injected through the round window membrane (see Materials and methods) to induce an osmotic shock to the hair cells (Chung et al., 2016).
evidence: Describes the experimental method used, supported by citation

claim: Recordings of ABRs in mice following intracochlear water instillation demonstrated minimal or no responses up to 75 dB SPL or higher.
source: Recordings of ABRs (Melcher et al., 1996; Biacabe et al., 2001) in mice following intracochlear water instillation demonstrated minimal or no responses up to 75 dB SPL or higher (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B

claim: ABRs to electric stimulation (eABRs) were generally similar to those reported previously in mice.
source: ABRs to electric stimulation (eABRs; Figure 3D) were generally similar to those reported previously in mice (Navntoft et al., 2019) and other laboratory animals (Miller et al., 1995), with multiple peaks occurring within the first few milliseconds following stimulus onset.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and citations to previous studies

claim: eABRs had multiple peaks occurring within the first few milliseconds following stimulus onset.
source: ABRs to electric stimulation (eABRs; Figure 3D) were generally similar to those reported previously in mice (Navntoft et al., 2019) and other laboratory animals (Miller et al., 1995), with multiple peaks occurring within the first few milliseconds following stimulus onset.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: ABR waveforms to magnetic stimulation (mABR) consisted of a number of peaks.
source: ABR waveforms to magnetic stimulation (mABR; Figure 3C) also consisted of a number of peaks, although the amplitudes of the early and later peaks were about the same.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The amplitudes of the early and later peaks in mABRs were about the same.
source: ABR waveforms to magnetic stimulation (mABR; Figure 3C) also consisted of a number of peaks, although the amplitudes of the early and later peaks were about the same.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The overall appearance of mABRs was closer to that of acoustically evoked ABRs vs. eABRs.
source: The overall appearance of mABRs was closer to that of acoustically evoked ABRs (aABRs) vs. eABRs, although we did not attempt to quantify this observation.
evidence: Based on qualitative observation from the experimental data

claim: The generation of robust ABRs to magnetic stimulation strongly suggested that micro-coils can drive the early auditory pathways.
source: Regardless, the generation of robust ABRs to magnetic stimulation strongly suggested that micro-coils can indeed drive the early auditory pathways, and therefore, we proceeded to collect responses from the IC.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data

claim: Magnetic stimulation elicited robust neural activity in the IC.
source: Consistent with the presence of robust mABRs, magnetic stimulation also elicited robust neural activity in the IC (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: Responses to magnetic stimulation were consistent with the tonotopic organization of the cochlea.
source: Responses to magnetic stimulation were consistent with the tonotopic organization of the cochlea.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Responses to stimulation of the basal turn were strong in the ventral portion of the IC, the region known to process high frequencies.
source: Responses to stimulation of the basal turn were strong in the ventral portion of the IC, the region known to process high frequencies, with little or no responses observed outside this region (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and established knowledge of IC tonotopy

claim: The average characteristic frequency for BSs in response to micro-coil-based stimulation of the basal turn was 37.36 ± 4.00 kHz.
source: Across animals (n = 6), the average characteristic frequency for BSs (extrapolated from Figure 2D) in response to micro-coil-based stimulation of the basal turn was 37.36 ± 4.00 kHz.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Magnetic stimulation of the apical turn elicited only a narrow portion in the dorsal portion of the IC, known to process lower sound frequencies.
source: In contrast, magnetic stimulation of the apical turn elicited only a narrow portion in the dorsal portion of the IC (Figure 4B), known to process lower sound frequencies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and established knowledge of IC tonotopy

claim: The characteristic frequency of the BSs for magnetic stimulation of the apical turn was 8.44 ± 6.58 kHz.
source: Averaging across the population, the characteristic frequency of the BSs for magnetic stimulation of the apical turn was 8.44 ± 6.58 kHz.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The spread of activation from electric stimulation was considerably wider than from magnetic stimulation.
source: In contrast to the relatively narrow spectral spread of IC activity arising from magnetic stimulation, the spread from electric stimulation was considerably wider (Figure 4C, D), consistent with findings in previous studies (Shannon, 1983; O'Leary et al., 1985, O'Leary et al., 2009, Micco and Richter, 2006; Middlebrooks and Snyder, 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D and citations to previous studies

claim: BSs for electric stimulation showed evidence of tonotopic organization.
source: Nevertheless, BSs again showed evidence of tonotopic organization, that is, stimulation of the basal turn was centered in the ventral portion of the IC while stimulation of the apex resulted in activation centered in the dorsal portion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: In all cases, the spread of activation from electric stimulation was wider than that from magnetic stimulation.
source: In all cases, that is, for both basal and apical stimulation and both d′ levels (moderate and high discrimination levels), the spread of activation from electric stimulation was wider than that from magnetic stimulation (Figure 5, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Table 1

claim: The difference in spread between electric and magnetic stimulation was significant for all stimulation locations, except for apical stimulation at d′ = 2.
source: This difference was significant for all stimulation location, except for apical stimulation at d′ = 2 (p = 0.8287; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: When the spread of magnetic stimulation was compared to that from auditory stimuli, there were no statistical differences for stimulation of the basal and apical turn.
source: When the spread of magnetic stimulation was compared to that from auditory stimuli, there were no statistical differences for stimulation of the basal and apical turn (both moderate and high discrimination levels) (p > 0.05, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: Eight of the nine STC profiles generated in response to electric stimulation exhibited two or more tips.
source: For example, eight of the nine STC profiles generated in response to electric stimulation exhibited two or more tips leading to an average of 2.33 per profile.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Seven of the nine STC profiles for magnetic stimulation had only a single peak tip.
source: In contrast, seven of the nine STC profiles for magnetic stimulation had only a single peak tip, with the remaining two profiles showing double tips (average of 1.22).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: All profiles for auditory stimulation had a single peak only.
source: All profiles for auditory stimulation had a single peak only.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The number of tips for electric stimulation was statistically higher than that from magnetic stimulation.
source: The number of tips for electric stimulation was statistically higher than that from magnetic stimulation (p = 0.007) or from acoustic stimulation (p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The difference between the number of tips for magnetic vs. acoustic stimulation was not statistically significant.
source: The difference between the number of tips for magnetic vs. acoustic stimulation was not statistically significant (p > 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The spread of activation was significantly narrower for magnetic vs. electric stimulation, regardless of the location at which stimulation was delivered.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the spread of activation was significantly narrower for magnetic vs. electric stimulation, regardless of the location at which stimulation was delivered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The narrower spectral spread from magnetic stimulation suggests the possibility that a coil-based CI may create narrower and more independent spectral channels.
source: While much additional testing is required, the narrower spectral spread from magnetic stimulation suggests the possibility that a coil-based CI may create narrower and more independent spectral channels, thus offering the potential for improved performance of an implant.
evidence: Based on inference and speculation from the experimental data

claim: The average DR across the population was smaller for magnetic stimulation (10.05 ± 4.18 dB V) than for acoustic stimulation (25.96 ± 9.17 dB SPL).
source: The average DR across the population was smaller for magnetic stimulation (10.05 ± 4.18 dB V, n = 6; basal stimulation, measured at the BS) than for acoustic stimulation (25.96 ± 9.17 dB SPL; 32 kHz tone; p < 0.001) but larger than that for electric stimulation (3.24 ± 0.99 dB mA; p = 0.0031) (Figure 6D), suggesting better discrimination resolution for stimulus intensity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The average DR for magnetic stimulation was larger than that for electric stimulation (3.24 ± 0.99 dB mA).
source: The average DR across the population was smaller for magnetic stimulation (10.05 ± 4.18 dB V, n = 6; basal stimulation, measured at the BS) than for acoustic stimulation (25.96 ± 9.17 dB SPL; 32 kHz tone; p < 0.001) but larger than that for electric stimulation (3.24 ± 0.99 dB mA; p = 0.0031) (Figure 6D), suggesting better discrimination resolution for stimulus intensity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The differences in DR did not arise from different neuronal response levels as the maximum response evoked by magnetic stimulation was comparable to that evoked by acoustic or electric stimulation.
source: The differences in DR did not arise from different neuronal response levels as the maximum response evoked by magnetic stimulation was comparable to that evoked by acoustic or electric stimulation, that is, no statistically significant differences between any pair of modalities (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: In some experiments with magnetic stimulation, response rates did not saturate, even at the maximum stimulation levels tested.
source: Note that in some experiments with magnetic stimulation, response rates did not saturate, even at the maximum stimulation levels tested here (Figure 6A), suggesting that the DRs reported here may be underestimated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The DRs for magnetic stimulation reported may be underestimated.
source: Note that in some experiments with magnetic stimulation, response rates did not saturate, even at the maximum stimulation levels tested here (Figure 6A), suggesting that the DRs reported here may be underestimated.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data

claim: Gentamicin caused a complete loss of outer hair cells and near complete loss of inner hair cells in the basal turn of the cochlea.
source: We applied a Gelfoam pledget soaked with gentamicin to the round window to cause a complete loss of outer hair cells and near complete loss of inner hair cells in the basal turn of the cochlea (Figure 7A, B; Heydt et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A, B and citation

claim: After 10 days of gentamicin treatment, DPOAEs were absent and ABR thresholds were beyond the range of the acoustic system or markedly increased (>75 dB SPL).
source: After 10 days, hearing was evaluated with acoustic ABR and distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs). DPOAEs were absent and ABR thresholds were beyond the range of the acoustic system or markedly increased (>75 dB SPL); a small amounts of residual ABR can arise from acoustic crosstalk from the contralateral unlesioned ear (Harrison et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation

claim: In gentamicin-treated animals, responses to electric and magnetic stimulation in the basal turn were robust.
source: In these gentamicin-treated animals (n = 2), responses to electric and magnetic stimulation in the basal turn were robust and spatial spread remained narrower in magnetic vs. electric stimulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Spatial spread remained narrower in magnetic vs. electric stimulation in gentamicin-treated animals.
source: In these gentamicin-treated animals (n = 2), responses to electric and magnetic stimulation in the basal turn were robust and spatial spread remained narrower in magnetic vs. electric stimulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Immunostaining in the basal turn at 32 kHz showed no remaining inner and outer hair cells.
source: Immunostaining in the basal turn at 32 kHz for hair cells (Myo7a, white) and actin-containing supporting structures (Phalloidin, red) showed no remaining inner and outer hair cells (Figure 7A), eliminating the possibility that observed responses to magnetic or electric stimulation arose from inadvertent activation of hair cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: The absence of hair cells eliminates the possibility that observed responses to magnetic or electric stimulation arose from inadvertent activation of hair cells.
source: Immunostaining in the basal turn at 32 kHz for hair cells (Myo7a, white) and actin-containing supporting structures (Phalloidin, red) showed no remaining inner and outer hair cells (Figure 7A), eliminating the possibility that observed responses to magnetic or electric stimulation arose from inadvertent activation of hair cells.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the experimental data

claim: Magnetic stimulation evoked multipeaked ABRs.
source: Magnetic stimulation evoked multipeaked ABRs, suggesting that coil-based stimulation was indeed capable of activating SGN processes that, in turn, led to activation of central nuclei in the auditory pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Coil-based stimulation was capable of activating SGN processes that led to activation of central nuclei in the auditory pathway.
source: Magnetic stimulation evoked multipeaked ABRs, suggesting that coil-based stimulation was indeed capable of activating SGN processes that, in turn, led to activation of central nuclei in the auditory pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data

claim: Multielectrode recordings obtained in the IC showed that responses were robust, narrowly confined, and tonotopically organized.
source: Multielectrode recordings obtained in the IC showed that responses were robust, narrowly confined, and tonotopically organized.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The responses from basal and apical micro-coil locations were narrow and showed little or no overlap between them.
source: The responses from basal and apical micro-coil locations were narrow and showed little or no overlap between them, whereas responses from electric stimulation showed considerable overlap for stimulation at the same locations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Responses from electric stimulation showed considerable overlap for stimulation at basal and apical locations.
source: The responses from basal and apical micro-coil locations were narrow and showed little or no overlap between them, whereas responses from electric stimulation showed considerable overlap for stimulation at the same locations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The number of peak tips observed in the ST profiles generated from the IC recordings was significantly lower for magnetic stimulation than for electric stimulation.
source: The number of peak tips observed in the ST profiles generated from the IC recordings was also significantly lower for magnetic stimulation than for electric stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The impedance from the coil to ground remained consistently above 200 MΩ.
source: First, the impedance from the coil to ground was monitored before and after each experiment and remained consistently above 200 MΩ, eliminating the possibility that observed responses arose from direct electrical activation, for example, from leakage of the stimulus current into the surrounding perilymph.
evidence: Describes control experiments performed in the study

claim: The DC resistance across the coil leads remained stable (<10 Ω).
source: Second, the direct current (DC resistance across the coil leads was also monitored regularly and it too remained stable (<10 Ω)), eliminating the possibility that a broken coil might be activating neurons capacitively.
evidence: Describes control experiments performed in the study

claim: Measurements of the temperature change produced by coils were previously shown to be less than 1°C.
source: Third, measurements of the temperature change produced by coils were previously shown to be less than 1°C (Lee et al., 2016; Ryu et al., 2020), greatly reducing the possibility that observed responses arose from some type of temperature shock.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The osmotic shock from DI water injection led to loss of responses to subsequent auditory stimuli, even at SPL levels of 75 dB.
source: The resulting osmotic shock led to loss of responses to subsequent auditory stimuli, even at SPL levels of 75 dB, strongly suggesting a loss of hair cell functionality.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The osmotic shock strongly suggests a loss of hair cell functionality.
source: The resulting osmotic shock led to loss of responses to subsequent auditory stimuli, even at SPL levels of 75 dB, strongly suggesting a loss of hair cell functionality.
